263	## 3. The nine steps, in short
264	
265	1. **The type theory.**
266	   - An F-bound, `I extends Integral[\I\]`, constrains the argument. It says nothing of `self`, which inside the trait is only an `Integral[\I\]`. Nothing makes every `Integral[\I\]` an `I`: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` satisfies the bound.
267	   - A body that treats `self` as an `I` is sound only under a further fact, which a language gets in one of four ways: a declared self type checked at each extender; a built-in `Self`; a closed world that lists `I` as the only member; or a run-time cast.
268	   - Greenman, Muehlboeck and Tate call these traits "shapes", and say they encode self types for "binary methods … as well as algebraic operations" (`reviews/mie-probes/literature.md:54`).
269	2. **What each path does today.**
270	   - The checker refuses the 30 (section 1).
271	   - Walk runs them: it has no static types.
272	   - The checker's self-type machinery exists, but only a `comprises` clause triggers it (way 5).
273	   - Walk overflows on such a clause (row 407). Walk's load check of `comprises` covers the main component only (row 551; `BuildEnvironments.java:1113-1330`).
274	3. **The specification.**
275	   - The type of `self` is the enclosing trait's type. With a `comprises` clause it is "T ∩ (U1 ∪ … ∪ Un)" (`Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex:53-69`, "% The new self-type idiom"; in the text by 2009-10-29, `7e6e40458`, Sukyoung Ryu). The meaning of way 5 is therefore already written.
276	   - A naked type variable may appear anywhere a type can, except in an `extends` clause, a `throws` clause or a wrapped field's type (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:66-73`). A `comprises` clause is not among the exceptions.
277	   - The traits chapter wants a listed reference to be "a declared trait identifier" (`traits.tex:163-165`), which a type variable is not. Victor Luchangco's note asks what the term covers (`:166-170`), and the revision left a bare variable open (decision record `:19`, `:48`).
278	   - The later Types chapter lets a clause list "types and generic types determined by the generic type of the declaration" (`types.tick:384-389`). Victor's comment there: "all the types in extends/excludes/comprises clauses must be trait types" (`:245`).
279	   - The type group's 2012 texts (the type group's late positions, which the curator weighs above the earlier text):
280	     - Welterweight types `self` as `T[P]` in a trait (`Papers/Welterweight/fig-wellformeddecls.tick:55`). It admits only constructed types in a clause (`fig-grammar.tick:6-8`, `:33-37`), and its self-typed dispatch step is commented out (`dispatch.tick:195-210`).
281	     - Naden: "The self-type idiom is realized with the comprises clause … the type Ring[X] is identified as X" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:580-582`), and he would have it "a separate construct which cannot be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds" (`:626-630`).
282	     - POPL 2019 has no self types (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md:280`, `:328-329`).
283	4. **Where it sits in the type system.**
284	   - The 30 ask one thing: the type of the variable `self` in a trait body.
285	   - Way 6 changes only that typing rule.
286	   - Way 5 changes more: through the clause it changes subtyping and exclusion (`Integral[\ZZ32\]` is `ZZ32`), which is why it touches walk and the overloading checks.
287	   - Way 2 leaves the types as they are and checks at run time. Ways 1, 3, 4, 7 and 8 rewrite the library so that the question does not arise.
288	5. **What the library does in the same family.**
289	   - `self` only in the self position (section 1, "What checks today").
290	   - `x.zero` and `x.one` (`:694`, `:710`).
291	   - The team's `cast` (`:33-37`), and a typecase on a trait's own parameter inside its functional method (`Contains.MATCH`, `:1093-1098`).
292	   - The witness typecase (`:2441-2446`).
293	   - Per-type algebra on the flat tower (`ZZ32`, `:734-750`), and the arrays' per-type `fill` (`:2276-2283`).
294	   - The compiler library's `comprises T` (`CompilerAlgebra.fsi:16`, `:24`).
295	   - The extenders that the default bodies serve: `String`, `Char`, `Boolean`, `Reflect.Type`, `CaseInsensitiveString`, `Comparison`, `Range`, `Vector`, `Matrix`, `Array1-3`, and programs' own (`ProjectFortress/tests/parametricManiaCompr.fss:20`, `XXXEmptyGroupSumRungF.fss:6`). The integer types declare their own orders.
296	6. **What the peers do.** Two families.
297	   - **A built-in self type.**
298	     - Rust: "`Self` … In a trait definition, it refers to the type implementing the trait" (*The Rust Reference*, Paths, "`Self`", https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/paths.html).
299	     - Swift's protocols have `Self` (not fetched).
300	     - Haskell's class defaults are typed at the instance, so the Prelude's `max x y` returns `x :: a` (Haskell 2010 Report, chapter 6, the `Ord` class; not fetched).
301	     - Under any of these the library's bodies check as written.
302	   - **An F-bound, `this` typed as the trait.**
303	     - Java uses `(T) this` or the "getThis" trick (FAQ206 above).
304	     - Scala declares a self type: "Inside the template, the type of `this` is assumed to be S"; "The self type of a class or object must conform to the self types of all classes which are inherited by the template" (*Scala Language Specification 2.13*, §5.1, Templates, https://www.scala-lang.org/files/archive/spec/2.13/05-classes-and-objects.html).
305	     - C#'s `INumber<TSelf>` declares its operators as static members over `TSelf` (literature note `:56`), which is way 7's shape.
306	     - Cecil, C#, Swift and Scala flatten the algebra (literature note §6).
307	   - Way 6 is Scala's rule. Way 5 is the closed-world form only Fortress has. Ways 2 and 3 are Java's.

309	   - 2008-08-21, Beckman's test diagnoses the swap (`6297a59c2`).
310	   - 2009-10-22, Ryu implements "the new self-type idiom proposal" (`3a8ad3b67`), and on 2009-10-29 adds the specification's paragraph (`7e6e40458`).

313	   - 2011-12-06, the compiler library has `Equality[\T\] comprises T` at its first reachable copy (`26718e298`, the ways note section 4).
314	   - The interpreter's library never carried a clause on these traits. Its bodies were only ever run by walk.
315	   - 2026: the flattening added `:685` and `:688-690` (`d846e3644`), the arrays' rung added `:2183-2190` (`f3b62bc83`), and batch 8 deferred the class (Q2).
316	8. **The derivation from his principles.**
317	   - "The library's own practice is the standard" puts ways 1 to 4 first. Of them, only way 2 reaches all three families without changing the api, and only way 4 reaches `:685` without a new device.
318	   - Route A, as the record reads it, weighs against way 5 and leaves way 6 open, since way 6 adds no clause and no exclusion. That reading is not POSITIONS' own words, so the question goes to him.
319	   - The type group's later word (Welterweight, Naden) weighs against a type variable in a clause (way 5), and Naden asks for a dedicated construct, which way 6 is.
320	   - "One global rule … from type theory and the peers" (POSITIONS, "No re-measuring what the record holds.") fits way 6, or way 5 as the team's own.
321	9. **The ways.** Section 2.

5	## The goal
6	
7	- **The measuring stick.** Finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification in `Specification/`, the Working Draft of 2010-12 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it; not redesign the language. The measure is one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast. A pure-Java microGPT is written later as the floor to measure against. The specification is a living document that reflects the changes we make. The tree is tagged `sealed-tree` at the map's last commit; commits after it edit the original sources, test-driven.
8	- **How he weighs his calls where the designers left no word.** "I don't care about type theoretical purity and I'm accepting all unfinished corners of the language because I want to get to a compiled version of micro GPT. And I think this is the right pragmatic approach so that we do not get bogged down in weeds. Theory. We want to get this one program running fast. That's our guiding star. But along the way, I want to stay true to the spirit of Fortress." He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and relies on the record: "I assume those people knew much more than I do right now." The check he asked for is a thorough top-tier review of every decision of his against the designers' intent, for errors of commission and of omission (`reviews/decisions-review/evidence.md`, `judgement.md`, `popl-recheck.md`); its items are decisions below.
9	- **The readable expression.** The toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression: "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources. The Hsu-style flat program gave "a few lumps of coal", not a diamond; the vocabulary is where any polishing happens. 71	- **Fixed-width overflow raises `IntegerOverflow` under `walk`** (row 379), as the specification says (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`, `:195-196`) and as the compiled path does: an overflow check in the natives of the interpreter's `Int` and `Long` glue classes raising the catchable `IntegerOverflow`, the unsigned `NN32` and `NN64` under the same rule. The code that means to wrap uses the specification's own wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` (unary and binary) and ⨰ `DOTTIMES` (`opr-overview.tex:172-176`, `:205-209`), declared on `Integral[\I\]` and on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ`, bound to wrapping natives of their own beside the checked ones, every expression fully parenthesised since their precedence is stated only among themselves; the strided distance that must not overflow is reordered and keeps the checked operators. Built (FACTS, "The specification's wrapping operators ∔, ∸ and ⨰ are declared in the interpreter's library" and "Under `walk`, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when the result does not fit"). The saturating family waits for a step of its own.
72	- **Mixed widths convert by declared coercions (answer 8).** Each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one, the compiler prelude's own pattern and the specification's ZZ32/ZZ64/ZZ128 example; `ZZ32` and integer literals coerce into `RR64` (exact); `ZZ64` into `RR64` stays explicit (lossy), by the integer principle; a generic call or range over mixed widths infers the narrowest type both sides coerce into, the promotion rule of the specification's inference chapter. The specification's `widens` is deferred. Built; no model line changed.
73	- **`NN32` coerces into `RR64`.** "if it fits, then there should be direct conversion. No question about it." — exact conversions are implicit, lossy ones explicit, answer 8's own criterion. One api line and one body line, a test, and the specification's callout on answer 8 reworded; in batch 8's library work, apart from the overloading work, since a new coercion changes which calls need one.
74	- **The numeral switch, split by where the static types are.** A numeral has a type of its own, `IntLiteral`, that each number type converts from, the compiler library's working version taken over the specification's unfinished numeral types: "walk needs to be corrected and switched to using IntLiteral." Q-lib, the one library taking the compiler library's `IntLiteral` model with `ZZ32`'s comparisons, PLAN item 33 and the `exactValue` case, with its S1 text, lands in batch 8 beside the `NN32`-to-`RR64` coercion; Q-walk, walk's numeral as an `IntLiteral`, lands after the switch-over's step that gives walk the checker's static types. Rows 79, 443, 437's walk half, 486, 395 and 511 go to Q-walk; row 454's integer half closes with Q-lib on the compiled path and its walk half with Q-walk, since walk's numeral reaches no `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` until then; item 33 (row 517) closes with Q-lib. Q-lib's brief quotes the team's warning whole ("Do not enable these until coercion is implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals.", `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:497-498`), and the rung measures where arithmetic lands under walk on the two microGPT programs and the interpreter tests before it lands, one measurement inside the rung.
75	- **Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only**, as the compiler library declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:173-174`): "ranges can realistically have only ever be ZZ32 because that's the largest array size on JVM". `RangeInternals` and the range operators of `FortressLibrary` have no integer type parameter, multi-dimensional ranges are tuples of `ZZ32` ranges, the public range traits stay generic in their index type; a range over another integer type is a static error; a wider counter is written as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index. Built.
76	- **`SUM` and `PROD` without the `Number` catch-all (answer 7).** One generic sum and one generic product reduction over the library's algebra bounds, each joined with the element type's own operator and taking its identity from the static argument through the library's `() -> T` witness `typecase` (the device of `array1`). The bare forms `SUM e`, `SUM vm` and `DOT` keep their text; a clause form whose element type nothing at the call fixes writes its static argument, as the team's tests do; the two model lines approved as diffs: `MicroGptFlat.fss:43` is `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] matCount(j)` and `:28`'s reduction is `BIG MAX z`. Built. Teaching walk to accept an unwritten static argument erased to `Bottom` is later work. The three `Number`-typed big operators `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN` are gone: the coercions need no rule about identities, since a sum's zero and a product's one carry into every wider type by themselves while a maximum's identity, the type's least element, does not; once `where` clauses work, the specification's own `HasIdentity` (`advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex:772-797`) could replace the witness `typecase` for `SUM`'s zero and `PROD`'s one, and `MAX` and `MIN` still get no identity on the integers or floats.
77	- **The team demos that write no static argument for a generic reduction** are respelled with their static arguments when a batch has a free slot, with a report-only demo stage; under the paper's instance rule the checker binds the bound instead of `Bottom` (row 425), so whether a demo runs unchanged is read again before the respelling. "Let's not touch them and we'll make them run later. If they will still need to be rewritten then ... then let's do it whenever."
78	- **The sign-refined number types are a superseded design.** The subtype lists of `basic-lib/numbers.tex` and `basic-lib/basic-integers.tex` are the library's run-time check methods (`check`/`check_star`, returning `Maybe`); `advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex` is kept word for word and marked as a superseded design, in the S1 form ("make sure we clearly record the original design"). Built. The Fortress form, native subtyping between instantiations ordered by flags together with multiple dispatch, has no mainstream counterpart; the covariant encoding is engineering, inferring the flags through arithmetic with no annotations is research.
79	
80	### Arrays and the model program
81	
82	- **Storage is `double[]`, unboxed.** "we must go to double array for performance. There is again no question about this. If this should have been high performance language, it cannot be boxed." The `nat` sizes are not sidestepped or layered in later: "That is a central design point that they are using." So the array fork and the `nat` fork are taken together: sized types as the team designed them, the checker taught `nat` parameters, in the library's own patterns.
83	- **The array design's three questions are open**, closed "as no decision taken": a store per element type chosen by the factory under the library's generic objects; the size also carried as a field on the store; a factory for a size known only at run time returning the unsized `Array`. None stands as a default; nothing was built on them. They return with the array design after the switch-over, through protocol § 6's method (a clean worker's list of every way the language and the library offer, the library's own way first, the nine steps), with the review's findings (`reviews/array-design-review.md`: the first refuted by probe, the second right and forced, the third stopping microGPT at the checker) and the ground moved since (one library; design B, whose factory can make a size's descriptor from a number known only at run time). The element width joins those questions: he asked why microGPT uses `RR64` and not `RR32`, LLMs being trained at FP32 at most; the reason on record is the Python reference's float64 goldens (`experiment/run-c-goldens/README.md`); not yet answered. The array decisions A (the mechanism that puts `double[]` under a float vector), B (where unboxed arithmetic happens) and D (sizes in the model's own types) stay after the switch-over, with plain explainers prepared beforehand.
84	- **The integration review's checks** (`reviews/numeric-hierarchy-integration-review.md`) stand for the array work: the generic `Vector`/`Matrix` bodies are checked per operation's required capability, with no blanket ring bound that would exclude integer arrays; the `SUM` replacement is accepted on the empty sum's type as well as its value; a tiny `PView`/transpose product, with its controls.
85	- **The model's text is the notation.** "NO. That's not Fortress!" An operator in the model does not become a function call to satisfy the interpreter's overload check. Any repair that would change a line of the model is shown to him as a diff before it is built, and the vocabulary is repaired around the notation, not the other way round. The sized signatures of C4's vocabulary, with every model line they force, are written as a diff shown to him (`reviews/decision-d-diff.md`), measured against microGPT's own checker errors; nothing is applied until phase 5. The ledger is one file; two views are derived from it.
86	- **The vocabulary's scalar drops and the diagonal.** The six scalar drops after the library's scalar block stand ("agreed. That is the plan"); the diagonal carries its own optimised product, as the type system promises: `Diag` extends `Matrix` and overrides `mul` (row 299 closed). A read-only matrix trait in the library (`ReadableArray2` under `Array2`) is a library change for a ledger row later, not a vocabulary hack.
87	- **`fill` takes a value, `tabulate` a function (answer 10).** The diamond is fixed by redeclaring `fill` in the leaf array traits, as the library does for `copy`, `map` and `replica`; the function form is named `tabulate` (after Scala's `Array.tabulate`), and `fill` keeps the value form, every peer's meaning of the word. Built; no model line changed.
88	- **`Maybe`'s empty case** (row 331). The team's parametric spelling `Nothing[\T\]` is the one library's, and the specification writes it so; the specification's bare non-parametric `Nothing` is future work gated on `where` clauses binding a type variable in an extends clause (unimplemented on both paths; the interpreter has no coercion alternative), not attempted before that gate opens; re-gating the row on static-argument inference is parked (`PLAN.md`).
89	- **What an object with no `asString` prints** (row 321): the bare Fortress type name, the interpreter's spelling, on both paths, through one native behind the compiled `Object.asString`; the debug marker he had in mind lives in `asDebugString`. Built; one case stays open on the row.
90	
91	### The specification's revision
92	
93	- **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** "our plan needs to update the spec with the change that we do and somehow properly record why we decided that way, so that there is no open discrepancy between the spec and our implementation that would be confusing to people. We need to preserve the original historic record somewhere in a document with our reasoning why we did the switch and preserve the option to go the route C." Every change takes the S1 form, an original-tree edit flagged as such; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is never touched.
94	- **The S1 form**, the layered form the team used for 1.0 and its 2009 draft: a labelled callout at each changed passage that prints in every build (not a `\note`); a revival section in Appendix I (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), each entry with the reason, the original sentences quoted with their path and line in the unrevised copy, and route C with what reversing to it would take; one paragraph in the front matter; the full reasoning in a repository document. The unrevised copy is called "the Working Draft of February 2011", in the team's own form, each citation giving the path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; Appendix I says once that the directory's name is misleading, since only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Appendix I's introduction says that the entries follow the revival's decisions, route A the first of them, each naming its own.
95	- **The refused examples (S2).** Each example the exclusion rule refuses is revised to the one library's shape, the original kept in the text as "Not allowed", the specification's own form, and the rule stated once in Luchangco's two-part form under "instantiation exclusion". Built. The `covariant` keyword gets one sentence in the revival callout at the covariance example, saying that the type group's later design declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, implemented on neither path, and pointing to the decision record and row 404. The number chapters (`basic-lib/basic-integers.tex`, `basic-lib/numbers.tex`, `advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`) changed in the same batch as the flattening, never earlier. The calculi of Appendix A (Core Fortress with Where Clauses, ACFFD and Basic Core) each carry a `\revision` callout saying that the calculus predates instantiation exclusion and admits the shapes the rule refuses, their rules and soundness claims untouched. The judgement's candidate ledger rows 2, 3 and 5 are parked (`PLAN.md`).
96	- **Appendix I's small items.** `TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]` in the api and the component, its five restated members kept, so that it gets back `MIN` and `MAX` (row 461 closed; built; taken on the coordinator's recommendation, and he wants it explained in more detail when he has the energy, "I need to pay that down", so it is on the list for his review).
97	
98	### How we work
99	
100	- **Test first, the test kept.** Every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to the corpus: the worker writes the test first, verifies that it actually fails, makes the fix, proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on; the full suite stays green. The unacceptable process is the one-off validation script, proving once by hand that the interpreter and the compiler agree and leaving no permanent check. The batches fix the issues the explorations captured as ledger rows, each with how to reproduce it, "Those are like our bug reports": the worker first commits the reproduction into the test suite, "this is how I have reproduced what the previous probe has discovered", then makes the fix, and the test passing demonstrates that the issue is fixed; "There isn't much more to it." The test captures the essence of the problem, not the shape the probe met it in, "do not blindly transpose the issue from the probe like think about it what's the core problem and capture that", written as a clean minimal version. Whether the test was seen failing first is read from the worker's transcript, not shown by a committed capture. The skeptic checks it there and runs no build to repeat it: "It should just check that the procedure of test first was followed. Not that it should be repeating the whole process, that is a fucking waste." Whether the suite runs per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per batch is in line with the rule. Every measured and repaired defect gets a gated assertion, a deferred spec-settled one an `XXX` test. The test needs no commit of its own: the order is test written, seen failing through the harness, the fix, the test seen passing, and the test and the fix may land in one commit ("I don't recall asking for test and fix to be separated into different commits ... I would worry about increasing the ceremony burden").

3	# The rule "put each extension into this library", with its context
4	
5	Written 2026-10-09 for the curator and the coordinating session. Revised the same day: §0 and §5 rewritten, §7 added, four lines fixed in place. Dates are 2026, times UTC. Every quotation of Pavol is verbatim from a transcript (speech-to-text slips kept), with the transcript and line it comes from.
6	
7	## 0. The short answer
8	
9	- **What he said on 2026-09-19 at 18:31.** "And the same goes with the micro GPT's use of like all, all the extensions that it invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Read alone, that covers every invention, the 26 operations and the 9 views included.
10	- **What it answered.** C4's operators were refused at load. The coordinator had just told him that the library lacked the float version of its own integer scalar extension (18:16) and an exclusion clause (18:22). At 17:01 he had assumed that C4 used the library's own arrays.
11	- **What he said when the broad reading was put to him.** On 09-20 at 06:42 the coordinator summed up his ruling as "Your ruling sends every invented extension into the library". He answered at 07:20 with a condition, not a yes. An extension needs "a precedent in the library itself". No "forms that are specific to our use case". Integer patterns extended to floats are "exactly what I will be after". And the model must show the library's worth: "It must be the other way around." At 13:57 he called the landed change "small defects in the library".
12	- **What he decided on 09-24.** The diagonal, one of C4's inventions, stays in C4's vocabulary as a `Matrix` with its own `mul`. A read-only matrix trait, which the library has at rank 1 and lacks at rank 2, is a library change for later.
13	- **So his words support a third reading.** The library is extended where its own text shows a gap: it has something for one number type, rank or sibling trait, and lacks it for another. The model's need is the occasion, not the reason. A form that only the model uses, with no such precedent, stays in the model's vocabulary unless he rules otherwise. He judges each extension.
14	- **His present reading** agrees in substance with 07:20, 13:57 and 09-24. It is narrower than 18:31, which said "all". It is a little narrower than 07:20, which accepted any extension with a precedent; his example there was the number type (integers to floats), not the rank.
15	- **The earlier text of this note** made 18:31 the rule and 07:20 its manner. Its restatement let a program's need decide where an extension goes, and said nothing goes into the program's own component. The diagonal decision says otherwise. §7 lists each difference.
16	- **`02d09a39f`** is mostly the kind of change he describes. It gave the library's one-dimensional integer `+ - MIN MAX` with a scalar to every number type and every rank, `Matrix` included. Two parts go past his description: number-minus-array, which is new, and the rank-3 exclusion of additive groups (§7, point 8).

19	## 1. 2026-09-15: the open question
20	
21	### Sources
22	
23	The 2026-09-15 exchange is not in the coordinating session's own transcript. That session (`fe616d40-…`) has records for 09-08, 09-09, 09-14, then 09-18 onward. The 09-15 session is the earlier archived one, `bdff267d-67dc-5bb9-b970-8c3dfaa634b6`, on the `transcripts` branch (`origin/transcripts`, `projects/-home-user-fortress/bdff267d-67dc-5bb9-b970-8c3dfaa634b6.jsonl.parts/001.jsonl`). 25	### What the extensions were
26	
27	The model program's vocabulary was a component of its own, `FlatArrays` (C4: `explorations/run-c4/src/FlatArrays.fsi` and `.fss`; the APL focused base had a smaller copy, `FlatArrays2`, in `apl/mg/`). The run's brief had told the worker that "everything you need beyond [the shipped library] is user-level code in your own component" (`explorations/reviews/c4-flatarrays-review.md` §2). The review of 2026-09-19 inventories it (`reviews/c4-flatarrays-review.md` §1): 38 declarations, of which 5 are aliases of library calls, 26 are new operations over the library's own `Array`, `Vector`, `Matrix` and `Array3`, and 9 are new structures (eight view objects and `Diag`). The 35 new things (26 operations and 9 structures), by family:
28	
29	| family | declarations (names in `FlatArrays.fsi`) |
30	|---|---|
31	| scalar extension of `RR64` arrays | `+` and `-` with a scalar in both orders, `MAX` with a scalar |
32	| elementwise algebra | `×`, `/` (array by array and by scalar), `>`, `SQRT`, `exp`, `log` |

7	## 1. The type question, in plain words
8	
9	Terms first.
10	
11	- A `comprises` clause closes a trait. `trait T comprises { A, B }` says `A` and `B` are the only types directly under `T`.
12	- `Integral[\I\]` is a generic trait, and its parameter is bounded by the trait itself ("F-bounded"): each integer type implements `Integral` at itself, `trait ZZ32 extends { AnyIntegral, Integral[\ZZ32\] }` (`.fsi:510`). It sits between the closed `AnyIntegral` and the five listed types, and it is not listed.
13	- Two readings of a clause. The type-level reading: the clause says which types may extend `T`. The value-level reading ("coverage"): the clause says where `T`'s values come from. A trait has no values of its own; only objects do.
14	
15	The question: does a closed trait that lists concrete types admit a generic, F-bounded subtrait? Each source, at its line:
16	
17	1. The rendered specification: no. A listed reference "is a declared trait identifier" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:161-165`), and the `Molecule` example forbids an unlisted trait to extend a closed one (`:262-279`). Victor Luchangco's draft note beside the first sentence asks whether the term includes "instantiations of parametric traits" (`:166-170`); the text never answers.
18	2. The draft note: no. "The traits listed in its comprises clause are exactly the traits that immediately extend T and they must explicitly extend T" (`traits.tex:234-246`). It is a `\note`, which a release build drops (`Specification/fortress/fortress.tex:35-36`). It restates Sukyoung Ryu's checker rule of 2009-04-17 and is in the draft by 2009-11-06 (ways note section 1); the Working Draft of February 2011 has it at `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex:231-234`.
19	3. The Types paper (OOPSLA 2011): no at the type level. "Any strict subtype of `C[\T\]` must also be a subtype of `[T/X]K_i` for some `K_i`" (`Papers/Types/exc-spec.tick:18-23`), and each listed `K_i` must be below `C[\T\]` (`:47-51`). `Integral[\ZZ32\]` is a strict subtype of `AnyIntegral` and above `ZZ32`, below none of the five, unless it is identified with `ZZ32`.
20	4. Karl Naden's journal text (2012; last touched 2012-08-31, `8015b17f4`): the identification is the self-type idiom. "The self-type idiom is realized with the comprises clause which contains the instantiation of the self type ... the type `Ring[\X\]` is identified as `X`" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:580-582`). With `Integral[\I\] ... comprises I`, `Integral[\ZZ32\]` is `ZZ32`, and the five-type list holds at the type level for the five.
21	5. The later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012-05-31, `275b90773`; `coordinator/spec-lineage.md:151-152`): yes, as coverage. A clause "specifies a set of types and generic types determined by the generic type of the declaration. An instantiation of the generic type defined by such a declaration is covered by the union of the types in this set and the corresponding instantiations of the generic types in this set" (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick:384-389`). `G` determines `G'` "if every parameter of `G'` is a parameter of `G`" (`:271-277`). So `AnyIntegral` may list the five and may not list `Integral`, which it does not determine. The chapter states no rule about extenders.
22	6. Welterweight (2012; in the tree by the import of 2012-07-19, `5a68404fd`): yes, at the value level. "The comprises clause, if present, indicates that no value can belong to the trait unless it also belongs to one of the comprised types" (`Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick:21-22`). Its rule D-Trait asks each listed type to be well formed and a subtype of the trait at the trait's own parameters, and asks nothing of the traits that extend it (`Papers/Welterweight/fig-wellformeddecls.tick:38-62`). Its grammar lets a clause hold constructed types only, never a bare type parameter (`fig-grammar.tick:6-8`, `:33-37`).
23	7. The compiled checker's rule (Ryu, 2009): no, unless the subtrait has a clause of its own. A trait extending a closed one must be below a listed type, or have a clause whose entries are each eligible (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:203-208`, `:254-266`); a type variable in that clause is filtered out (`:262`), so `comprises I` makes any generic subtrait eligible. The rule's own statement is the team's test `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/Compiled10.i.fss` ("(3) Eligibility to extend").
24	
25	Which is the designers' latest word. The decision of 2026-09-23 weighs the type group's later, implementation-informed word above the specification's earlier text; the decision of 2026-09-26 names the later Types chapter as the designers' later word wherever it covers a topic (POSITIONS 2026-09-23, 2026-09-26, the lineage note). The chapter covers this one (`types.tick:384-389`), and Welterweight, the group's 2012 calculus, reads the clause the same way. Naden's sentence of the same year is the type-level reading, in a paper about the return type rule; his idiom and the coverage reading agree on every value and differ only on whether a valueless trait may sit between. So the answer: yes. A closed trait that lists concrete types admits a generic subtrait, on the condition that every value below the generic subtrait belongs to a listed type. `AnyIntegral`'s clause meets it: only the five extend an instantiation of `Integral` anywhere in the tree (ways note section 1, the grep). The checker's rule is the group's earlier reading. It is the rule that made Ryu delete the team's own clause in 2009 ("Fixed comprises clauses in libraries", `3d2849cef`) and leave the comment that records what was meant, "not yet: comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]" (`.fsi:434`; Jan-Willem Maessen's message of 2008-07-02, "we can't write a comprises clause that mentions Integral[\I\]", `82c85b03a`, ways note section 4). The five-type list is that closure written the only way the later chapter allows.
26	
27	One fact every reading shares. A program's own `trait MyIntegral extends Integral[\MyIntegral\] end` with an object makes the list false. Measured: the checker accepts that program with 0 errors on the tree, under `comprises I`, and under both accommodations; only the 2008 clause on `Integral[\I\]` refuses it (ways note section 1, `anyintegral-comprises-ways/captures/probes/user-integral.txt`). The checker checks immediate subtypes only, so the hole is at every closed level of the tower, not at this clause. Under Welterweight values come from objects (its rule D-Object, `fig-wellformeddecls.tick:66-`), so the sound check is at an object declaration: an object below a closed trait must be below a listed type. That is a ledger row, not this decision.

131	## For Pavol
132	
133	**Question.** How do we resolve the checker's refusal of `AnyIntegral`'s `comprises` clause, the last early error in the `FortressLibrary` api?
134	
135	**Context.**
136	
137	- Refresher. `trait T comprises { A, B }` closes `T`: `A` and `B` are the only types directly under it. The design has it so two traits can be told apart without a `where` clause: closed families that share no member exclude each other, which lets an operator be overloaded on both.
138	- The shape. `AnyIntegral` is the marker "some integer type" and lists the five integer types. `Integral[\I\]`, the generic interface each integer type implements at itself, sits between them, unlisted. The checker wants every direct child listed; `Integral` cannot be, being generic, and the team's `where` spelling (their "not yet" comment on the line) is unimplemented.
139	- What the designers said. The 2008 text and the checker's 2009 rule: a child must be listed. The record (FACTS, POSITIONS, the ledger, INDEX and the notes) is the project's memory, kept in the repository because a session can move to another container; `fortress-repo` defines it near its top, with its files, and the `coordinator` skill picks each worker's slice of it, so that the dependency runs one way and a worker never needs the `coordinator` skill. How a Claude Code session behaves (long commands, waits, interrupts, the permission check) belongs in `fortress-repo`, which every worker has loaded, not in a skill of its own; what only the coordinator needs of it goes to `coordinator`. The checker count and the distance are the ladder's metrics: the workflow's prompts say how to run them and the `coordinator` skill names them; `fortress-repo` holds nothing of them. `fortress-repo` carries no batch structure, on purpose: which roles exist, who builds, checks, runs the gate, commits and pushes to `main` are set by whoever writes the workflow or the brief, so that agents designing a workflow from the skill are not steered toward ours; the skill says how to do each thing, and the brief says which an agent does. The role split may later be written as behaviours a batch's instructions point to, in a skill of its own. An agent acts on its brief alone: the skill names no other authority over what it commits or pushes, and no rule an agent cannot act on (it cannot ask him). A worker works with three things, its brief, the record and the original tree, in one of two modes: building, where it stands on the record and carries out its mission, and exploring, where it has met something the record does not settle (a gap, two of the team's sources in conflict, new evidence against a decision), gathers evidence in the record first and then in the original tree, adds what it found to the record and returns to building. Where the team's sources disagree, the later one wins, the specification included. A worker never settles such a conflict itself, and never revises the specification to a later source on its own reading: the conflict is surfaced, and the curator rules after research by the nine steps; a decision on record is carried out, and questioned only on evidence the decision did not use. A conflict between the text and an implementation that no decision settles gets a ledger row and a test of the current behaviour; an `XXX` test belongs to repair work, where the current behaviour is tolerated for a time on purpose and the test is promoted once the fix is in. What a worker builds on while its question waits for him is left unsaid: it is case by case, and a reversible choice takes the path of least resistance without a rule. An agent takes the tree it starts from as green, starts with its own failing test, reuses only what its brief cites or its own work ran, and runs more only where its edit reaches; test first applies to an edit of source code. A point a brief wants reviewed is a "point to report", never a "stop", which reads as a condition that stops the worker. A skill's parts are written by the seven writing principles (`explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`), which he has read and judged safe to apply to every rewrite: the writer applies them to a whole part at once, and he then reads it, not comment by comment. The earlier lenses note and the review-style profile are not a writer's brief. Before he reads a rewritten part, a cold reader given only the skill reads it as the workers who use it would, flags each passage that would send it wrong or make it search, with its confidence, the undefined terms and the gotchas; the coordinator reviews the findings, the writer fixes them with his comments so far, and only then does he read it. A comment on the review page marks a problem area, not a sentence to patch: the fix is made at the level of its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind. The skills are rewritten in place, git holding the earlier text. One writer does the writing, briefed by the coordinator, every comment fix on the page among its tasks, made from the coordinator's brief of his comment instead of the coordinator interpreting his words: it edits the skill files and commits them, and the coordinator keeps the review page in step, so that the writer's context holds only the writing. The writer is a headless Claude session (`explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, its standing brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`), since such a session keeps its prompt cache for an hour, as the coordinating session does, while an Agent-tool subagent keeps it for five minutes and so writes its whole context again when the curator's next comment comes later than that; the cache's one-hour writes cost more and are worth it. It is resumed for each writing task, and started fresh with only its standing brief when its history no longer serves, as after a large pass or the coordinator's compaction. Its standing order: ASD-STE100 at least halfway, terms defined first and then used, concise procedures, positive phrasing; and it does not take the register of what it reads, since FACTS, POSITIONS and many notes were written by earlier models in agent shorthand that the curator cannot follow cold, and the coordinator, which carries them in context, keeps drifting into it. A writer's minor decisions not taken are settled by the coordinator from the record, as his executive assistant, and not put to him; he is asked only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter. A position's bold title here is the record's handle, not his words, and is never quoted to him as his. A glossary of terms, in a skill or on a page, is written as a dictionary is: each term and the noun phrase that opens its definition with no article ("revival", not "the revival").
133	- **The statement for the public record on the usage limit.** "let the public record state that I'm now doing unpaid testing job of Anthropic's cloud infrastructure in my open source repository that is normally doing open source research of agentic coding capabilities." The account's weekly limit on all models stopped a running batch after its rung workers; later turns and subagents were served while the limit still read reached; he did not activate the promotional credit the panel offered, and his reading since is that visiting its page activated it unknowingly and that the work served was the $250 promotional credit for the cloud product, support having told him the offer had expired, "which was not true" (`coordinator/usage-metering-2026-09-30.md`, "After the report"); the container was booted afresh at each wake once nothing kept the session busy; at his word the batch was resumed to see whether it survives such interruptions and finishes.
134	
135	## How he wants to be spoken to
136	
137	- **The register.** "Drop the smart Alec essayist register before I blow a fuse": plain sentences, no framing flourishes, no closing lines that sum up in a phrase; advice as instructions, not as observations; replies very brief, plain English, no internal jargon. A wall of text is one he cannot absorb; the failure mode "is focused on over-compressing into a clever turn of phrase, but utterly fails in communicating clearly." Label which part answers which question when several are asked; do not restate what is in this file or in FACTS.md; when a concept is new to him, define it (he asked for reshape, ravel, planes, gather, outer product, Ring, Field, nat parameters, matrix multiplication).
138	- **Asks and decisions.** Decisions are presented one at a time as: what we do, what it changes, with a default he can accept without reading the argument; the argument lives in the committed review, not in chat. An ask for a yes states, in the message itself, what the worker would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what it costs, what the yes commits him to afterwards and what a no costs ("What are the consequences of the yeses? What does that work even want to do? ... this is just pressuring me to give approval without understanding"); one ask per message; no label stands in for an explanation, and a new name is defined in the sentence that uses it; the recommendation comes after the explanation, in one line, never instead of it.
139	- **Ownership.** "I need to maintain some ownership of this work, even if we are doing agentic coding … I did not know what you did. I need to know what you did. And I need to be aware of those choices and decisions because I am the one carrying the responsibility for the consequences as a director of this revival": every re-approval row is gone through in detail, grouped by theme, and the count of reversals is not the measure. A decision made inside a worker's report and recorded in one line is a decision not made; flag it to him at the time.
140	- **The coordinator's standing goal** is to model what Pavol already knows and where his context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the minimal set of relevant facts at the level he needs to decide; machine tokens are spent on thinking so that human context is protected. This came out of a compaction that left him "out of control, unaware of crucial details" while the coordinator was "taking unauthorized initiative which compounded my sense of helplessness to steer the Fortress revival efforts". The coordinator's two hats: "executive assistant here in this Fortress Revival project, helping me, the director, find a way forward, and the analyst that finds out what the fuck happened, why, and how do we move forward".
141	- **While a batch runs**, no progress reports on it until it lands. He is on Central European time; check-in times are given to him in UTC and in his local time. The harness's stop-hook reminders about uncommitted or unpushed work are processed silently, declined without a word while work is in flight, and never mentioned to him. He reads on an iOS client that sometimes shows stale state; "is anything in flight" is answered from the tree, not from the UI.
142	- **Format.** "table formatted in this way is hard to read on mobile … we just need a list": no tables in chat, lists. "write the numbers just as K or M. I'm fine as a programmer understanding what a kilo is": never spelled-out thousands and millions, and a numbers message carries few numbers, each with its meaning. Time is spoken from the clock or the record (when a batch will probably land, when a check-in fires), never from feel, "yesterday", "this morning", "last night", when the events were minutes or hours apart (protocol § 3). On his phone he reads a page while iOS's Speak reads it aloud at a fast rate, so every page for him has a Select button beside each larger section's heading that selects that section's text for Speak; a section's evidence and references are gathered at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points, and the Select button leaves them out, so that listening never runs through citations.
143

=== FACTS entries ===
47:- **The exclusion fork, priced three ways and dated** (five notes under `reviews/mie-probes/`). On these prices Pavol chose to keep the rule, route A (POSITIONS, "The exclusion rule stays and the tower is flat"). *Dated* (`spec-sentences-dated.md`): the spec's sentence that overloads may not differ in static parameters is 2009 text (Sukyoung Ryu, before the rule entered the checker in 2010) never revised; the passages allowing double membership are 2008-2009 text untouched through 2012; only the advanced chapter's meet-rule preamble was rewritten in 2010, author lost; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is not a genuine 2008 snapshot for three of these files. *Keep the rule* (`price-keep-the-rule.md`, `keep/`): 14 declaration headers flattened the compiler prelude's way (`Number` loses its algebra and 52 catch-alls, `RR64` takes the algebra on); 367 sites certainly needed a conversion (160 library, 207 in 35 test files; microGPT 37 through `Number`'s catch-alls), measured by an observing shadow over all 392 interpreter tests; the interpreter needs coercion called at dispatch (`OverloadedFunction.bestMatch`'s "TODO add checks for COERCE", about 150-200 lines in six files, run-time choice where the spec's is static); and a defect found on the way, a `ZZ64` bound to a numeral doing 32-bit arithmetic (row 146). All of it is built (the entries under Landed semantics). *Drop the rule* (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md`, `scope/`): the dispatcher is already loaded under the call site's static arguments and only its arms read the value; making the arms use the dispatcher's own arguments is 43 lines in `OverloadSet.java` (since built for template dispatchers), under which `MieDispatchSub`, refused by the checker as a double member of `Tag`, compiles with the rule relaxed and answers `Marker[Blue]`, the compiler prelude byte-identical, all 43 generic-overload compiler tests printing the same; not built for dotted and functional methods, `opr`/`nat`; the spec's overload sentence enforced refuses 179 library api pairs under the narrow reading and 335 under the wide one, which refuses the tower's own method implementations; padding a family to one parameter list passes on both paths; 6 compiler and 6 interpreter tests refused; symbolic operators, never examined by the checker, add 329 pairs; the spec also says (`overloading.tex:173-175`) static parameters are inferred before applicability for dynamic calls, citing what was then an empty chapter. *Literature* (`literature.md`): the Fortress group kept the rule after 2012 (Welterweight 2012; POPL 2019, whose [Anc-Same-Trait] is the rule, blanket for an invariant parameter, and whose run-time check of the return type chooses the instance, never the declaration: "The team's latest word on types and on the exclusion rule is the unfinished restart, not `Specification/`" under The specification and the repository's lineage); Java, Kotlin, Scala, X10 keep it with flat numbers; C#, F#, Rust, Haskell allow double membership and choose statically; Julia avoids it by single inheritance and gives up static soundness; nobody published a resolution under run-time dispatch nor a proof the rule is necessary. *The 2012 patents' forest rule* (`patents-forest-rule.md`, `forest/`; US 8,843,887 col. 8 l. 8-12, US 8,898,632 col. 8 l. 23-27, Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, Luchangco, filed 2012-08-31): a self-typed generic (one that "comprises exactly T") may be carried at several instantiations if they form a chain; in a shadow `checkP` accepting the library's F-bound as the test it lifted 48 of the nested tower's 61 exclusion errors (tower 31, comparisons 7, `Maybe` 10; the reductions' 13 stay, `DistributesOver` is not self-typed); under the patents' literal `comprises T` test nothing is lifted, no library trait has the clause (`CompilerAlgebra.fsi:16, :24` do); it does not close the specialisation hole (a specialisation at `Mid` catches `Narrow` values; calls typed `Eq[Narrow]` die with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`), which needs a covariant reading (one POPL 2019's [D-Method] denies the tower: a self-typed algebra trait's parameter stands in a parameter position, so `Equality[\+T\]` is ill formed; `reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md` § 1.1), dispatch agreeing with it, a return-type rule over every level below a specialisation (40-70 lines, derived, not in the patents), the call-site fix, and seven library declarations completed; Welterweight's `static.tick:83-89` states the blanket rule and its self-typed dispatch step is commented out. What the checker reports on the flat library today is the gate's ("The checker-count stage's table" and "The true distance to the switch-over" below).
48:- **Route C built whole as a shadow: the forest rule closes the specialisation hole only with a return-type rule over every level of a chain, and switching to C costs more than the record said** (`reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md`, patches, run script and captures under `reviews/mie-probes/route-c/`, on the nested tower). C-full (the forest with the library's F-bound taken as self-typed, the covariant reading, a return-type rule derived from Naden's general form with one instance per level of the chain, levels above included, a more specific declaration covering a level, 109 lines; the call-site fix of `scope-call-site-dispatch.md` verbatim) is 5 files, 188 code lines: the three hole probes are refused at compile time instead of dying with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`, the completed programs link and give walk's answers, no dispatch change is needed beyond the call-site fix; all 43 generic-overload compiler tests print the same, 7 differ in classes and 22 compiler-prelude classes differ under the forest switch alone, untraced; the gate was not run. On the nested library the gate's instrument could not see the rule (the `FortressLibrary` api stopped at its hierarchy stage: 37 under forest, C-full and C-lite alike, 24 with the `DistributesOver` markers dropped); the deep instrument (the zero stack) shows the rule refusing 25 pairs at 21 declarations (`ZZ64`'s fifteen letter-named operators at level `ZZ32`; `Number`'s and `QQ`'s `MIN`/`MAX`/`MINMAX`), and seven declarations complete the tower (`TIMES` on `ZZ32`; `MIN`/`MAX`/`MINMAX` generic in `Integral` and on `NN32`), after which nothing is refused, but only when `Integral[\ZZ32\]` is identified with `ZZ32`, which the patents license through `comprises T` alone, and `comprises T` on the eight self-typed traits (`LexicographicOrder` must carry it too) overflows the checker in `Formula.tImplies`/`primImp` (`Formula.scala:185-205`), with the rule dropped as well. Three things no checker rule reaches: a chain with no specialisation dies compiled with `AbstractMethodError`, because the code generator writes no forwarding method for a middle level's instantiation (`CodeGen.java:891-899`, read from the error, not traced; route B would meet it too); the checker infers the top of a chain and walk the bottom, so the two paths answer differently on one program; the interpreter refuses the specialised pairs and overflows on `comprises T`. C-lite (a specialisation only at a leaf of its chain) refuses 28 pairs at 23 declarations, the tower's inner half (`ZZ64`'s operators and `CMP`, `Number`'s and `QQ`'s `MIN` family and `CMP`), so it costs the inner levels their specialised bodies; symbolic operators escape both rules. In-betweens supported: C's checker half inert beside route A (on the flat library it gives the stock checker's errors, error for error, `route-c/flat-count.txt`); the flat-widths hybrid (unmeasured); C-lite at the cost named. Killed: the forest without the rule; a rule over the levels below only (`ForestLeafInv`, `VerifyError`); the patents' literal `comprises T` in today's checker. What reversing route A to C would cost, to which the route decision points (POSITIONS, "The exclusion rule stays and the tower is flat"): C is probeable as a shadow and its checker half is additive, but switching also needs the call-site fix, a per-level method in the code generator, interpreter work, a way past the overflow, and the seven declarations on top of un-flattening.
56:- **The true distance to the switch-over, measured on today's tree: on the flat library the checker reports 1,736 distinct errors under walk's setting and 1,527 under the compile path's, of which the gate's count shows 62** (`perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance-flat.md`, scripts and captures under `perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance-flat/`; on the nested tower the totals were 2,523 and 2,359, `perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance.md`). The title's figures are that measurement's, on an earlier flat library. The last landed gate reads 153 under the gate's setting `any`, the bound `Any` with compiled-expression desugaring (POSITIONS, "The implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter is `Any`"), and a count of 1 (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-12/gate/distance.txt`, `checker-count.txt`, `summary.txt`); walk's setting and the compile path's own `extends Object` setting are not measured by the gate. Over twelve prelude apis and their twelve components, the overloading memo off, in one JVM (`DistanceMulti.java`), the 153 are: exclusion 0; `comprises` 0; overloading 2; return type 2; abstract method not implemented 0; the `extends Object` bound 0; other well-formedness 17; component bodies' type errors 129; export mismatches 3 (`distance.txt:3-11`; by root cause in the next entry). Each landed batch's movement by kind, unit and class is in its gate's `summary.txt` and its `distance` lines, under `compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/`, and is read in its record's last section ("The landing" or "The gate") or, where the record has none, in its review's first section (`reviews/batch-*-review.md`). The stage's three crash rows (`distance.txt:32-34`) are of kind `TypeError`, one cause: the checker refuses a local function's omitted parameter type, "Missing parameter type for i", in `__bigOperator`'s `body(i)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1304`) and in the `asString` of the rank-2 and rank-3 array traits, at `row(i)` (`:2500`) and `row(i,k)` (`:2899`), where the local function is bound (`STypeEnv.scala:69-77`; Appendix I, "The type of a parameter that a declaration leaves out"; rows 620 and 621 fixed, 622 a duplicate of 621; "Crashes reach zero in the shadow ..." above; the checker's crash on them without the refusal, "Type is not inferred" and "TryChecker returned an untyped expr", in `compile-ladder/rung-checker-defects/REPORT.md` section 5). The refusals uncover no error the distance counts (`reviews/batch-11-review.md` section 1). `Stream`'s variance stage reads a varargs parameter's element type and does not crash (row 623; "The compiled checker types a varargs parameter as the team's `ImmutableArray[\T, ZZ32\]` ..." below). Code generation, measured once by the title's measurement: `FortressLibrary` emits 326 declarations and refuses 225, 4 of them on declarations the checker passed; the overload rewriting's `BottomType` stop is gone; the dispatch generator finishes and refuses 12 of 198 overload sets (131 of 283 on the nested tower). The count stage runs walk's setting (by reading its code) and sees 1 of the distance's 153; its per-api rows count each error twice (`FortressLibrary` 2 against the total 1). The count stage runs the `FortressLibrary` api's overloading and return-type checks, which `StaticChecker` skips while a unit has an earlier error (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java:268-272`); the api's last early error, `AnyIntegral`'s `comprises` clause, is cleared ("The tower closure of `02d09a39f` has no spelling the compiler's checker accepts" below). Those checks add 1 error, the overloading of `isLeftZero` in `LexicographicReduction` (`compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`), counted twice and already counted by the distance stage. A zero count is necessary, not sufficient (`coordinator/library-route-judgement.md:33`). In addition, every trait except \TYP{Any} and \TYP{Object}

We define the extension relation to be the transitive closure
of implicit and
explicit extension.
That is, trait \VAR{T} \emph{extends} trait \VAR{U}
if and only if \VAR{T} explicitly or implicitly
extends \VAR{U} or if there is some trait \VAR{S}
that \VAR{T} explicitly extends and that extends \VAR{U}.
The extension relation induced by a program is the smallest
relation satisfying these conditions.
This relation must form an acyclic hierarchy
rooted at trait \TYP{Object}.
\note{
Victor: Technically, there may be self cycles in explicit extension due to

If a trait \VAR{T} extends trait \VAR{U},
or if \VAR{T} and \VAR{U} are the same trait,
we say that \VAR{T} is a subtrait of \VAR{U}
and that \VAR{U} is a supertrait of \VAR{T}.

We say that trait \VAR{T} \emph{strictly extends} trait \VAR{U}
if and only if
(\emph{i}) \VAR{T} extends \VAR{U} and (\emph{ii}) \VAR{T} is not \VAR{U}.
We say that trait \VAR{T} \emph{immediately extends} trait \VAR{U}
\note{
Victor: I think we don't use ``immediately extends'' anywhere in the spec,

if and only if (\emph{i}) \VAR{T} strictly extends \VAR{U} and
(\emph{ii}) there is no trait \VAR{V}
such that \VAR{T} strictly extends \VAR{V}
and \VAR{V} strictly extends \VAR{U}.
We call \VAR{U} an \emph{immediate supertrait} of \VAR{T}
and \VAR{T} an \emph{immediate subtrait} of \VAR{U}.
\note{Victor: this belongs in the type chapter.}

A trait with an \KWD{excludes} clause excludes
every trait listed in its \KWD{excludes} clause.
If a trait \VAR{T} excludes a trait \VAR{U},
the two traits are mutually exclusive:
neither can extend the other, and no trait can extend them both.
As discussed in \secref{type-relations},
the exclusion relation is symmetric.
Thus, if \VAR{T} excludes \VAR{U}
then \VAR{U} excludes \VAR{T}
whether or not \VAR{T} is listed in an \KWD{excludes} clause
in the declaration of \VAR{U}.

If a trait declaration of \VAR{T} includes a \KWD{comprises} clause
then every type listed in its \KWD{comprises} clause extends \VAR{T},

\subsubsection{Exception for selfless types}

This restriction is problematic for expressing certain types of relationships such as the numeric hierarchy
that is expressed using the so called self-type idiom (now selfless types or trolls). Some sets of numbers
and the operators over them give rise to special algebraic properties known as rings and the more specialized fields.  Fortress
aims to support them in the following way:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\bf trait}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~\dots~{\bf end}\\
{\bf trait}~{\tt Field}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~{\bf extends}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~\dots~{\bf end}
\end{array}$\\

The self-type idiom is realized with the {\bf comprises} clause which contains the instantiation of the self type.
The {\bf comprises} clause limits the types that can extend the given type to those appearing in the clause.
In this idiomatic usage, the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{X}$ is identified as $X$.  Thus a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
is really just $\mathbb{Q}$ itself.

Unfortunately, the numerical hierarchy contains crossed instantiations of the kind that we determined
must be outlawed:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\bf trait}~\mathbb{Q}~{\bf extends}~{\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}~\ldots~{\bf end}\\
{\bf trait}~\mathbb{Z}~{\bf extends}~\{ \mathbb{Q}, {\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}\}~\ldots~{\bf end}\\
\end{array}$\\

A $\mathbb{Z}$ is a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$ and a ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ but not
a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ which breaks our rule given above.  As above, we can come
up with an example that is unsound if we allow this type hierarchy.\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it add}\ob{X}({\tt Ring}\ob{X}, {\tt Ring}\ob{X}) :{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it add}\ob{Y}({\tt Field}\ob{Y},{\tt Field}\ob{Y}) : {\tt Field}\ob{Y}~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

Take type $\mathbb{Z}$ which is provided as the inputs to {\it add}.  Both {\it def1} and {\it def2}
are applicable.  But if we instantiate {\it def1}
at $\mathbb{Z}$, then we have a return type of ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ for the less specific
definition.  The more specific {\it def2} is only applicable when instantiated at $\mathbb{Q}$, but the
resulting return type ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not a subtype of ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$,
thus witnessing the failure of the return type rule.

Recall that the return type rule handles two failure cases: first, the possibility that more specific
type information at runtime will cause a more specific function definition to be chosen.  Second
is that the more specific function may not be visible to the compiler (hidden behind an API).  Note
that the first failure case should not actually apply here.  When we statically know that we have
a ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$, we actually know much more than this.  The self-type idiom means
that this type is equivalent to $\mathbb{Z}$.  But $\mathbb{Z} <: \mathbb{Q} <: {\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
which implies that based on static information {\it def2} should apply.  However, this does not extend to
the second failure case when the more specific definition is hidden.

One way to ensure that the first situation cannot happen is to rewrite the overload so that the self-type
is a bound rather than the parameter type:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it add}\ob{X <:{\tt Ring}\ob{X}}(X,X) : X~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it add}\ob{Y <: {\tt Field}\ob{Y}}(Y,Y) : Y~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

This forces us to recognize the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ as $\mathbb{Z}$ in order for {\it def1} to
apply which will automatically also mean that {\it def2} applies.  This approach suggests further that
the self-type idiom should be more than simply an idiom and instead a separate construct which cannot
be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds.  Victor and John have started working on this
sort of theory with their {\it trolls}.  However, the visibility problem shows that this is not sufficient to fix the
unsoundness problems with the cross instantiation.  Therefore, more work needs to be done in order
to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy in the Fortress type system.

# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:

         git push origin main
         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
         git push origin main:blinded-fable

     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.

# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them.

A FACTS entry is the fact, its source and its test in a few lines, under a bold title. It points to the report that holds the detail. Cite it by its bold title, or by its opening words if it has no title.

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Add a fact to FACTS in the commit that establishes it, as a new entry in the section of its topic. Its source and its test can be the code at file:line, a gated test, or a command and its output. If your brief does not let you write FACTS, put the entry in your report as finished prose.

- POSITIONS holds the curator's decisions, in the curator's words, written once. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

    opr <(self, other:Self): Boolean = LessThan = (self CMP other)
    opr >(self, other:Self): Boolean = other < self
    opr =(self, other:Self): Boolean = EqualTo = (self CMP other)
    opr <=(self, other:Self): Boolean = other >= self
    opr >=(self, other:Self): Boolean = (self = other OR: self > other)
end

(** %StandardMin% is a MIN operator; most types that implement %MIN%
    will implement a corresponding total order.  It's a separate type
    to account for the existence of floating point numbers, for which
    NaN counts as a bottom that is less than anything else but doesn't
    actually participate in the standard total ordering.  It is
    otherwise the case that %a MIN b = a% when %a <= b% and that
    %a MIN b = b MIN a%. **)
trait StandardMin[\T extends StandardMin[\T\]\]
    opr MIN(self, other:T): T
end


(** StandardTotalOrder is the usual total order using <,>,<=,>=,=, and
    CMP.  Most values that define a comparison should do so using
    this.  Minimal complete definition: either CMP or < (it's
    advisable to define = in the latter case).  As noted above, %MIN%
    and %MAX% respect the total order and are defined in the obvious
    way. **)
trait StandardTotalOrder[\Self extends StandardTotalOrder[\Self\]\]
        extends { StandardPartialOrder[\Self\], StandardMinMax[\Self\] }
    opr CMP(self, other:Self): TotalComparison =
        if self < other then LessThan
        elif other < self then GreaterThan
        else EqualTo
        end
    opr >=(self, other:Self): Boolean = NOT (self < other)
    opr <=(self, other:Self): Boolean = NOT (other < self)
    opr MIN(self, other:Self): Self = if other < self then other else self end
    opr MAX(self, other:Self): Self = if other < self then self else other end
    opr MINMAX(self, other:Self): (Self,Self) =
        if other < self then (other, self) else (self, other) end
end
